summary:
Aguascalientes is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework. Its own trans-specific provisions are thin: Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records that Aguascalientes "has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people", and its reporting of 31 March 2025 places the state among those that have not legislated such a procedure. There is consequently no state-level administrative mechanism for changing name or gender markers on official records.

The human-rights cost of that absence is documented by Human Rights Watch in its March 2024 report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society", which uses Tabasco to show how non-reforming states, Aguascalientes among them, leave trans people without any lawful marker procedure and with identity documents that do not match their lived identity.

A court-ordered route exists alongside the legislative gap. Infobae reported on 9 April 2026 that Mexico's Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 with a project by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, held the Aguascalientes Civil Code requirements for gender change on birth certificates, namely judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations, to be discriminatory and a violation of privacy. The Court ordered the state's Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, issuing a new birth certificate with no marginal notes revealing a prior gender. The ruling's immediate effect is limited to the persons represented by the civil association that filed the amparo, so Aguascalientes has a court-ordered administrative recognition route in the absence of legislative reform.

On homicide, Aguascalientes has adopted no transfemicide offence. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City made transfemicide a criminal offence; Aguascalientes is one of the states that have introduced no comparable reform.

Local activists document continuing harm. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem of Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente say conversion-therapy operations still run in Aguascalientes under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one of these spaces reached the group last year. The same activists state that trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression in the state.

The ENDISEG survey shows 7.3% of the state's population aged 15 and over self-identifies as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest proportion among Mexico's states.
tangentialFactors:
Aguascalientes sits at the non-reforming end of a national spectrum that Human Rights Watch mapped on 31 March 2025, where recognition procedures exist in some states and not others; the state's own position is the specific finding, while the wider distribution is carried by the national record.

Tabasco serves as the documented comparator for what non-reform means in practice: the Human Rights Watch report of March 2024 uses that state to illustrate the consequences Aguascalientes shares, namely the absence of any lawful procedure for aligning identity documents.

Mexico City's transfemicide law of July 2024 provides the clearest contrast on criminal-law protection, and Aguascalientes is among the states that have not followed it.

Aguascalientes' 7.3% LGBTI+ self-identification rate is the fifth-highest among Mexican states, which places a comparatively visible population against a legislature that has enacted neither recognition nor transfemicide reform.
localsOnly:
Residents of Aguascalientes have no legislative procedure for legal gender recognition; the only route documented in the sources is the administrative one the Supreme Court ordered the state Civil Registry to provide, and the Court's ruling took effect for the persons represented by the civil association that brought the amparo.

Conversion-therapy provision is prohibited by law but, according to Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem, operations continue in the state under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes. One person who escaped such a space approached the group in 2025.

Trans women in Aguascalientes continue to face aggression motivated by prejudice, as reported by the same activists to La Jornada Aguascalientes on 23 August 2026.

State-level identification data: the ENDISEG survey records 7.3% of residents aged 15 and over as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest share among Mexican states.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Aguascalientes Civil Registry has extended the confidential administrative recognition procedure ordered by the Supreme Court to people beyond the amparo's named plaintiffs, and whether any legislative reform bill on gender recognition is before the state Congress. The sources do not say.

Unresolved: whether any conversion-therapy operation in Aguascalientes has been investigated, closed or prosecuted since the prohibition took effect. The inventory records only the activists' assertion that such operations persist.

Not sourced: there is no state-specific record in this inventory of killings of trans people in Aguascalientes, of hate-crime prosecutions, or of the state's complaint-handling practice for anti-trans violence. National and other-state figures belong to the parent record.

Unresolved: the date on which the Supreme Court's Aguascalientes ruling became generally enforceable and the practical availability of the Civil Registry route for a person without legal representation.
